# Introduction

**Keycloak Admin** is a .NET client library that provides comprehensive access to **Keycloak administration APIs.**
This library simplifies the integration with Keycloak servers, offering a clean and intuitive interface for managing
users, clients, roles, and more.

## From Where it Started?

We needed an easy way to integrate with Keycloak in .NET projects and tried existing Keycloak client libraries.
Unfortunately, they were missing several important things that we needed, so we forked the
original [Keycloak.NET from Silent Partner Software](https://github.com/silentpartnersoftware/Keycloak.Net), and started
to improve it.

Over time, we added many features and enhancements, leading to the **Keycloak Admin** as a library of its own.

# Improvements

- Fully integrated with dependency injection. Added `KeycloakService` that serves to create needed 
  `IKeycloakAdminClient` instances (with `basic auth`,
  `client secret`, `token`) and can be easily injected into your services using dependency injection.
- **Centralized token caching** across all requests (using `MemoryCache`)
- Thread-safe token acquisition
- **Automatic/Lazy token refresh** only when needed (Reduced network calls to Keycloak)
- **Secure token storage [cache]** using `SecureToken` class (using `SecureString`)
- Automatic token disposal when evicted from the cache
- Removed `Flurl` dependency (uses `HttpClient` instead directly).
- All Keycloak models are now immutable (records) to ensure thread safety.
- Removed support for the older Keycloak API style (without `/auth` path).
- **.NET Aspire integration** for quick setup.
- **.NET Aspire for testing**. No need to set up anything to test! Run the tests, and they will use Aspire to mock the
  Keycloak API.
- Generates coverage report and full HTML coverage documentation.
- **Single file apps for running tests and Nuget packaging** (no more ugly scripts, everything is in C#). -- **Note:**
  needs **.NET 10** installed --


- Each `IKeycloakAdminClient` instance **nicely separates subjects** (e.g. `IKeycloakAdminClient.Users`,
  `IKeycloakAdminClient.Clients`, etc.) to avoid confusion and make it easier to use.
  ⚡Available categories:
  - `AttackDetection` - Security and brute force detection
  - `AuthenticationManagement` - Authentication flows
  - `ClientAttributeCertificate` - Certificate management
  - `ClientInitialAccess` - Client registration
  - `ClientRegistrationPolicy` - Registration policies
  - `ClientRoleMappings` - Client role mappings
  - `Clients` - Client management
  - `ClientScopes` - Client scopes
  - `Components` - Component management
  - `Groups` - Group management
  - `IdentityProviders` - Identity providers
  - `Key` - Key management
  - `ProtocolMappers` - Protocol mappers
  - `RealmsAdmin` - Realm administration
  - `RoleMapper` - Role mappings
  - `Roles` - Role management
  - `RolesById` - Role operations by ID
  - `ScopeMappings` - Scope mappings
  - `ServerInfo` - Server information
  - `Users` - User management
  - `UserStorageProvider` - User storage providers

The `Six.KeycloakAdmin` repository uses GitHub Actions workflows to automate critical development processes including 
continuous integration, testing, and quality assurance. These workflows ensure code quality, maintain consistent build 
processes, and provide immediate feedback on pull requests and code changes.


# PR Test Workflow
----
The **PR Test Workflow** (`pr-test.yml`) is the primary quality gate for all pull requests targeting the `main` branch. 
This workflow automatically builds the solution, runs comprehensive tests, generates coverage reports, and provides 
detailed feedback to developers before code can be merged.

**When it runs:**
- ✅ **Pull Request Opened**: Triggers on new PRs targeting `main`
- ✅ **Pull Request Updated**: Runs on every commit pushed to PR branches
- ✅ **Pull Request Synchronized**: Executes when PR is updated with new commits
- ❌ **Direct Push to Main**: Does not run on direct commits to `main` (protected branch)


### Coverage Analysis and Reporting
The workflow includes a coverage analysis step that measures how much of the codebase is tested by the unit tests. 
This helps maintain high code quality and ensures that new changes do not introduce untested code.

**Coverage Features:**
- **Instrumentation**: Instruments code for coverage measurement
- **Data Collection**: Gathers execution data during test runs
- **Coverage Reports**: Generates detailed coverage metrics
- **Quality Metrics**: Ensures adequate test coverage

**Report Generation:**
- **Data Processing**: Analyzes collected coverage data
- **Report Formats**: Generates multiple report formats (HTML, XML, etc.)
- **Quality Gates**: Applies coverage thresholds and rules
- **Artifact Preparation**: Prepares reports for upload

**Artifact Management:**
- **Conditional Upload**: `if: always()` ensures upload even on failure
- **Retention**: Keeps artifacts for 30 days for analysis


# GitHub Pages Deployment Workflow
----
The **GitHub Pages Deployment Workflow** (`deploy-gh-pages.yml`) automatically builds and deploys the project 
documentation to GitHub Pages whenever changes are pushed to the `main` branch. This ensures that the documentation 
is always up-to-date with the latest code changes.

- ✅ **Manual Trigger**: Can be manually executed from the GitHub Actions tab
- ❌ **Pull Requests**: Does not run on PRs (only on main branch pushes)

- Deploy to the `github-pages` environment with proper permissions

The workflow requires specific permissions to function properly:

- **Pages**: Write access to deploy to GitHub Pages
- **ID Token**: Write access for secure authentication during deployment

- **Insurance**

    If for some reason you want to change the credentials, **you need to make sure both realms have the **same 
    username and password** as the tests use the same credentials for both master and Insurance realms.**
</Aside>

# Overview

The `Six.KeycloakAdmin` project uses an automated NuGet mini-packaging system that streamlines the entire process from 
source code to published packages. This system automatically discovers all library projects, builds them with optimized configurations, creates properly versioned NuGet packages, and publishes them to your specified feeds with minimal manual intervention.

<Aside>
    CSharp File based apps **need .NET 10 installed.**

    Download the latest .NET 10 SDK from the official [.NET download
    page](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/download/dotnet/10.0).
</Aside>


# Packing & Publishing

The NuGet packaging system provides three distinct publishing workflows, each designed for specific use cases and environments. Each workflow automatically handles versioning, dependency resolution, package signing, and metadata generation according to industry best practices.

<Aside>
    **Environment Configuration for NuGet Publishing**

    The packaging system requires specific environment variables to be configured based on your publishing targets.
    Configure only the variables needed for your intended distribution strategy:

    - `DEV_LOCAL_NUGET_FEED_URL` - Directory path for local development feed storage
    - `PRIVATE_NUGET_FEED_URL` - Endpoint for your private NuGet feed
    - `PRIVATE_NUGET_FEED_PAT` - Personal Access Token (PAT) for private feed authentication
    - `PUBLIC_NUGET_FEED_PAT` - Personal Access Token (PAT) for `NuGet.org` publishing

    **Note:** For local-only publishing, only `DEV_LOCAL_NUGET_FEED_URL` is required. Additional variables are
    automatically detected and used when present.
</Aside>

## To local (development) feed

Local development feeds are ideal for testing packages during development, sharing with team members, or validating package behavior before wider distribution. This workflow creates packages optimized for development scenarios with enhanced debugging information and local path resolution.

```
# Pack and publish to loval development feed (default)
dotnet run build/nuget-pack.cs

# One can also specify the local feed path explicitly
dotnet run build/nuget-pack.cs --local
```

## To private remote feed

Private remote feeds enable secure distribution of packages within your organization or to trusted partners (for 
example, to private GitHub repositories).

```
# Pack and publish to private feed
dotnet run build/nuget-pack.cs --private
```

## To public remote feed

Public distribution to **NuGet.org** represents the final stage of package maturity, making your libraries available to 
the global .NET community.

```
# Pack and publish to public NuGet.org
dotnet run build/nuget-pack.cs --public
```


## Build Configuration Options

The packaging system defaults to Release configuration for optimal performance and production-ready packages. However, you can override this behavior for specific testing or debugging scenarios where additional diagnostic information is required.

```
# Pack with debug configuration
dotnet run build/nuget-pack.cs --debug
```


# Additional Configuration (In-Script)

The packaging script automatically discovers projects to package, but you can customize this behavior by modifying the script configuration directly. This is useful when you have specific project organization requirements or need to exclude certain projects from packaging.

### Search Directories

By default, the script searches for projects in the `libs` directory. You can modify the `searchDirectories` list to include additional directories or change the search scope:

``` csharp
// In build/nuget-pack.cs
var searchDirectories = new List<string>
{
    "libs",           // Default library projects
    "tools",          // Additional tools directory
    "extensions"      // Custom extensions directory
};
```

### Ignored Projects

You can specify projects that should be excluded from packaging by adding their full project names to the `ignoredProjects` list:

``` csharp
// In build/nuget-pack.cs
var ignoredProjects = new List<string>
{
    "Six.Example.TestProject",        // Exclude test projects
    "Six.Example.BenchmarkProject",   // Exclude benchmark projects
    "Six.Example.ExperimentalProject" // Exclude experimental features
};
```

**Note:** Project names should match the exact filename without the `.csproj` extension. The script automatically filters out these projects during discovery, ensuring they are not included in the packaging process.

# What is AGENTS.md?

[AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) is a standardized markdown file that contains project-specific instructions, context, and guidelines
specifically designed for AI coding agents.

While README.md files are written for humans with quick starts, project descriptions, and contribution guidelines,
**`AGENTS.md` complements this by containing the extra, sometimes detailed context coding agents need: build steps,
tests, and conventions that might clutter a README or aren't relevant to human contributors.**

The format was intentionally kept separate to:
- **Give agents a clear, predictable place for instructions**
- **Keep READMEs concise and focused on human contributors**
- **Provide precise, agent-focused guidance** that complements existing README and docs

<Aside type="note">
    **Open Format**: AGENTS.md is an open, community-driven format. If you're building or using coding agents and find
    this helpful, feel free to adopt and contribute to its evolution.

    See more at [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/)
</Aside>


# AGENTS.md in this Template

The **Six Solution Template** includes a comprehensive `AGENTS.md` file that provides detailed guidance for AI coding
agents working with .NET C# projects. This file serves as the authoritative source for project-specific context and instructions.

<Aside type="tip">
    **90% Ready-to-Use**: The `AGENTS.md` file in this template is essentially complete and covers all the features
    that the **Six Solution Template** provides. You basically only need to modify the **🏗️ Project Overview** section to
    describe your specific project instead of the template itself.

    All other sections (setup commands, testing instructions, NuGet packaging, documentation workflows, code standards,
    etc.) are already configured and ready to use as-is for your .NET project.
</Aside>


# Key Sections in Our AGENTS.md

## 🏗️ Project Overview
Explains that **Six Solution Template** is a GitHub template repository for creating .NET C# projects with professional
tooling, automated workflows, and documentation setup.

## 🚀 Setup Commands
Provides both automated and manual setup instructions, including:
- Prerequisites (.NET 10 SDK, Docker, Git)
- Automated setup using `setup.cs`
- Manual configuration steps
- Essential development commands

## 🧪 Testing Instructions
Comprehensive testing guidance including:
- Commands for running tests with coverage
- Test project structure and organization
- Coverage requirements and reporting

## 📦 NuGet Packaging
Detailed instructions for package creation and publishing:
- Environment variable configuration
- Packaging commands for different environments
- Package metadata management

## 📚 Documentation
Documentation system guidance:
- Astro.js Starlight with Six theme
- Content structure and organization
- Development and deployment workflows



# Best Practices

## Content Guidelines

<Steps>

    1. **Be Specific and Actionable** - Provide exact commands and clear instructions rather than vague descriptions.

    2. **Include Context** - Explain why certain practices or tools are used, not just how to use them.

    3. **Keep It Current** - Treat AGENTS.md as living documentation that evolves with your project.

    4. **Focus on Agent Needs** - Include information that agents need but might not be obvious to humans.

</Steps>

## Organization Tips

- **Use Clear Headings** - Organize content with descriptive section headers
- **Provide Examples** - Include code examples and command samples
- **Link to Resources** - Reference external documentation when appropriate
- **Version Control** - Keep AGENTS.md in version control alongside your code

<Aside type="danger">
    **Avoid Sensitive Information**: Never include API keys, passwords, or other sensitive data in AGENTS.md. Use
    environment variables and reference them in the instructions.
</Aside>


# Large Projects and Monorepos

For large monorepos or projects with multiple components, you can use **nested AGENTS.md files** for subprojects. Place an AGENTS.md file inside each package or subproject directory. Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence.

## Example Structure

```
MyProject/
├── AGENTS.md                    # Main project instructions
├── frontend/
│   ├── AGENTS.md               # Frontend-specific instructions
│   └── src/...
├── backend/
│   ├── AGENTS.md               # Backend-specific instructions
│   └── src/...
└── docs/
    ├── AGENTS.md               # Documentation-specific instructions
    └── content/...
```

This approach allows each subproject to have tailored instructions while maintaining overall project guidance.


# Maintaining AGENTS.md

**Living Documentation**: The most effective AGENTS.md files are those that are actively maintained and updated as
the project evolves. Regular maintenance ensures agents always have current, accurate information.



# Resources

For more information about AGENTS.md:

- **Official Site**: [agents.md](https://agents.md/) - Complete documentation and examples

# Introduction

The template uses a centralized `Nuget.config` file that defines four distinct package sources:

1. **Local Feed** - For local testing and development (could also be used as a development feed I team shares a
common directory; for example, on One Drive or similar)
2. **Development Feed** - For development packages
3. **Staging Feed** - For staging packages
4. **Production Feed** - For production releases (for example, if the package is free, on NuGet.org)

<Aside type="tip">
    All configuration values (feed urls, usernames and secrets [personal access tokens]) **are stored as environment
    variables**, ensuring security and flexibility across different development environments.

    See more how to configure them in the [NuGet Secrets](./nuget-secrets/) documentation.
</Aside>




# Feed Configuration

The `Nuget.config` file is located in the solution root and contains:

```xml
<configuration>
```

# Overview

The `Six.SolutionTemplate` uses environment variables to securely manage NuGet feed credentials, ensuring that 
sensitive information like **Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and usernames are never committed to source control.**

This approach provides maximum security and flexibility across different development environments while maintaining ease of use.

## Why Environment Variables?

Environment variables offer several critical advantages for credential management:

- **Security**: Credentials are stored outside source code, preventing accidental exposure in version control
- **Flexibility**: Different environments (development, staging, production) can use different credentials without code changes
- **Team Collaboration**: Each developer can configure their own credentials without affecting others
- **CI/CD Integration**: Build systems can securely inject credentials during automated processes

## Credential Types

The template supports four distinct feed types, each with its own set of credentials:

1. **Local Feed** - No credentials required, uses the local directory path only
2. **Development Feed** - Requires URL, username, and PAT for team collaboration
3. **Staging Feed** - Requires URL, username, and PAT for pre-production testing
4. **Production Feed** - Requires URL, username, and PAT for final releases (e.g., NuGet.org)

</Aside>

| `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_URL` | Production NuGet feed URL |
| `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_USERNAME` | Username for production feed |
| `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_PAT` | Personal Access Token for production feed |

# Overview

This guide covers how to create and manage documentation for your .NET project using **Astro.js Starlight** with the **Six theme**. You'll learn how to create new documentation pages, use Astro components, organize content, and configure the sidebar navigation.

The documentation system is built on:
- **Astro.js**: Modern static site generator
- **Starlight**: Documentation-focused Astro theme
- **Six Theme**: Custom theme from Six Technology

<Aside type="tip">
    **Quick Start**: Documentation files are located in `docs/src/content/docs/` and use either `.md` or `.mdx`
    extensions. The `.mdx` format allows you to use React-like components within your content.

    This solution template uses the [Six theme](https://github.com/six-tech/Six.StarlightTheme),
    which is a custom theme built on top of Starlight. It provides a clean, modern look with additional components and
    styling options.
</Aside>

# Creating New Documentation Pages

## File Structure and Naming

Documentation pages are organized in the `docs/src/content/docs/` directory. For example:

```
docs/src/content/docs/
├── introduction.md                    → /introduction/
├── setup-and-configuration.md         → /setup-and-configuration/
├── nuget/
│   ├── nuget-secrets.mdx              → /nuget/nuget-secrets/
│   ├── nuget-feeds.mdx                → /nuget/nuget-feeds/
│   └── nuget-publish.mdx              → /nuget/nuget-publish/
└── project-documentation/
    ├── setting-up-documentation.mdx   → /project-documentation/setting-up-documentation/
    └── creating-documentation.mdx     → /project-documentation/creating-documentation/
```

## Page Frontmatter

Every documentation page must start with **YAML frontmatter** that defines the page metadata:

```yaml
---
title: Page Title                    # Required: Appears in browser tab and navigation
description: Page description        # Required: Used for SEO and page previews
sidebar:
  label: Custom Sidebar Label       # Optional: Override sidebar display name
  order: 10                        # Optional: Control sidebar ordering
  hidden: false                    # Optional: Hide from sidebar navigation
  attrs:
    class: special-page            # Optional: Add CSS classes
draft: false                       # Optional: Mark as draft (hidden in production)
---
```

<Aside type="tip">
    **Required Fields**: Both `title` and `description` are required for all documentation pages. Missing these will
    cause build errors.
</Aside>



# Configuring Sidebar Navigation

The sidebar navigation is configured in the `astro.config.mjs` file. Here's how to add your new documentation pages:

## Understanding the Sidebar Structure

The sidebar is organized into groups with items:

```javascript
sidebar: [
    {
        label: 'Getting Started',           // Group label
        items: [
            {label: 'Introduction', slug: 'introduction'},
            {label: 'Setup and Configuration', slug: 'setup-and-configuration'},
        ],
    },
    {
        label: 'Testing',                   // Another group
        items: [
            {label: 'Running Tests', slug: 'testing/running-tests'},
        ],
    },
]
```

## Adding New Pages

<Steps>

    1. **Identify the appropriate group** - Decide which existing group your page belongs to, or if you need to create a
    new group.

    2. **Add the page to the group** - Add a new item object to the appropriate group's `items` array:    
    `{label: 'Creating Documentation', slug: 'project-documentation/creating-documentation'}`

    3. **Create new groups if needed** - If your page doesn't fit into existing groups, create a new group with the
    appropriate label and items array.

</Steps>

### Example Configuration

Here's how to add a page to an existing group:

```javascript
{
    label: 'Creating Documentation',
    slug: 'project-documentation/creating-documentation'
}
```

And here's how to create a new group:

```javascript
{
    label: 'New Section',
    items: [
        {label: 'New Page', slug: 'new-section/new-page'},
    ],
}
```

## Advanced Sidebar Configuration

You can also configure individual sidebar items with additional options:

```javascript
{
    label: 'Advanced Guide',
    slug: 'advanced/guide',
    attrs: {
        class: 'advanced-item',         // Add CSS classes
        target: '_blank'                // Open in new tab
    }
}
```

For external links in the sidebar:

```javascript
{
    label: 'External Resource',
    link: 'https://external-site.com',
    attrs: {
        target: '_blank',
        rel: 'noopener'
    }
}
```


# Working with Assets and Images

## Adding Images

Place images in the `docs/src/assets/` directory and reference them using relative paths:

```markdown
![Description](../../assets/image-name.png)
```

For the Six theme, you can use hero images:

```markdown
![Six Hero](../../assets/six-csharp-template-banner-wide-1980-01.png)
```

# Purpose

The NuGet packaging script automates package management by:
- **Project Discovery**: Automatically finds all library projects in the solution
- **Build and Pack**: Builds projects and creates NuGet packages
- **Multi-Feed Support**: Publishes to local, development, staging, and production feeds
- **Environment Configuration**: Uses environment variables for secure configuration
- **Symbol Packages**: Creates and publishes symbol packages for debugging

# Package Creation Process

The script automatically discovers library projects by:
- Scanning the `libs/` directory
- Looking for `*.csproj` files
- Excluding ignored projects
- Handling project dependencies


# Usage

```bash
# Package to local feed (default)
dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs

# Package to local feed (explicit)
dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --local

# Package to development feed
dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --dev

# Package to staging feed
dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --staging

# Package to production feed
dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --prod
```

## Arguments

| Argument                   | Description                                |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `--local` or no argument   | Package to local feed                      |
| `--dev` or `--development` | Package to development feed                |
| `--staging`                | Package to staging feed                    |
| `--prod` or `--production` | Package to production feed                 |
| `--debug`                  | Use Debug configuration instead of Release |

<Aside type="tip">
    Currently, the version must be bumped manually in the `libs/Directory.Build.props` file.
</Aside>


# Environment Configuration

The NuGet packaging system provides four distinct publishing workflows, each designed for specific use cases and environments.

Therefore, the script requires specific environment variables to be configured based on your publishing targets.

Therefore, please read about how NuGet feeds are configured and how to manage secrets here:

## NuGet Publishing Workflows

<Aside type="tip">
    #### Local Feed (Default)
    
    - **Purpose**: Development and testing    
    - **Behavior**: Copies packages to local directory
    - **Use Case**: Local development, testing, and validation

    ```bash
    # Pack and publish to local development feed (default)
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs

    # One can also specify the local feed path explicitly
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --local
    ```    
</Aside>
<Aside type="tip">
    #### Development Feed
    
    - **Purpose**: Internal development and testing
    - **Behavior**: Publishes to development NuGet feed
    - **Use Case**: Team development, integration testing
    
    - `NUGET_FEED_DEV_URL` - Endpoint for your development NuGet feed
    - `NUGET_FEED_DEV_USERNAME` - Username for development feed authentication
    - `NUGET_FEED_DEV_PAT` - Personal Access Token (PAT) for development feed authentication

    ```bash
    # Pack and publish to development feed
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --dev
    # or
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --development
    ```
</Aside>

<Aside type="tip">
    #### Staging Feed

    - **Purpose**: Pre-production validation
    - **Behavior**: Publishes to staging NuGet feed
    - **Use Case**: Pre-release validation, stakeholder testing
    
    - `NUGET_FEED_STAGING_URL` - Endpoint for your staging NuGet feed
    - `NUGET_FEED_STAGING_USERNAME` - Username for staging feed authentication
    - `NUGET_FEED_STAGING_PAT` - Personal Access Token (PAT) for staging feed authentication

    ```bash
    # Pack and publish to staging feed
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --staging
    ```
</Aside>

<Aside type="tip">
    #### Production Feed

    - **Purpose**: Public distribution
    - **Behavior**: Publishes to production NuGet feed (e.g., NuGet.org)
    - **Use Case**: Public releases, production distribution
    
    - `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_URL` - Endpoint for your production NuGet feed (e.g., NuGet.org)
    - `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_USERNAME` - Username for production feed authentication
    - `NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_PAT` - Personal Access Token (PAT) for production feed authentication

    ```bash
    # Pack and publish to production feed (e.g., NuGet.org)
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --prod
    # or
    dotnet run scripts/nuget-pack.cs --production
    ```

    **Note:** For local-only publishing, only `NUGET_FEED_LOCAL_URL` is required. Additional variables are
    automatically detected and used when present.
</Aside>

- **Directory Structure Standardization**
- **Configuration Standardization**
- **Standardization by Templates**

# Introduction

The **Six Solution Template** provides a set of predefined configuration files that handle the most important 
aspects of .NET development.

This page explains each configuration file, what it configures, and how to customize it for your specific needs.

<Aside type="tip">
    Most configuration files work out of the box. Only modify them when you have specific requirements that differ from the template defaults.
</Aside>


# Directory.Build.props

The template implements a hierarchical MSBuild configuration system using `Directory.Build.props` files. 
This creates a layered approach where settings cascade from general to specific, ensuring consistency while allowing customization.

## Root Directory.Build.props

The master configuration file **in the solution root** establishes baseline settings for all projects:

```xml
<!-- Root Directory.Build.props - Master configuration -->
<Project>
<PropertyGroup>
    <LangVersion>13</LangVersion>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
</PropertyGroup>

    <!-- StyleCop configuration -->
    <PropertyGroup>
        <CodeAnalysisRuleSet>$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)rules.ruleset</CodeAnalysisRuleSet>
        <StyleCopTreatErrorsAsWarnings>false</StyleCopTreatErrorsAsWarnings>
    </PropertyGroup>

    <!-- CI/CD optimizations -->
    <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(CI)' == 'true'">
        <ContinuousIntegrationBuild>true</ContinuousIntegrationBuild>
        <Deterministic>true</Deterministic>
    </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

**What it configures**:
- **Language version** (C# 13)
- **Code quality settings** (nullable types, warnings as errors)
- **StyleCop integration** for code style enforcement
- **CI/CD optimizations** for deterministic builds

## Project-Specific Directory.Build.props

Individual directories contain specialized configurations:

### libs/Directory.Build.props

```xml
<!-- libs/Directory.Build.props - Library-specific settings -->
<Project>
    <Import Project="$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)../Directory.Build.props" />

    <PropertyGroup>
        <IsPackable>true</IsPackable>
        <GeneratePackageOnBuild>false</GeneratePackageOnBuild>
        <IncludeSymbols>true</IncludeSymbols>
        <SymbolPackageFormat>snupkg</SymbolPackageFormat>
    </PropertyGroup>

    <!-- Source Link for debugging -->
    <ItemGroup>
        <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub" Version="8.0.0" PrivateAssets="All" />
    </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

**What it configures**:
- **NuGet packaging** settings for libraries
- **Symbol packages** for debugging support
- **Source Link** integration for source code debugging

### tests/Directory.Build.props

```xml
<!-- tests/Directory.Build.props - Test-specific settings -->
<Project>
    <Import Project="$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)../Directory.Build.props" />

    <PropertyGroup>
        <IsPackable>false</IsPackable>
        <IsTestProject>true</IsTestProject>
    </PropertyGroup>

    <!-- Code coverage configuration -->
    <PropertyGroup>
        <CollectCoverage>true</CollectCoverage>
        <CoverletOutputFormat>cobertura;html</CoverletOutputFormat>
        <Threshold>80</Threshold>
    </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

**What it configures**:
- **Test project identification** for build systems
- **Code coverage collection** settings
- **Coverage thresholds** and output formats

## How the Hierarchy Works

The configuration hierarchy follows this pattern:

1. **Root Directory.Build.props** - Base settings for all projects
2. **Directory-specific Directory.Build.props** - Specialized settings that import and extend the root
3. **Individual project files** - Final customizations for specific projects

```xml
<!-- Example: A library project inherits from both levels -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
    <!-- This automatically imports ../Directory.Build.props -->
    <!-- Which in turn imports ../../Directory.Build.props -->

    <PropertyGroup>
        <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
        <!-- Project-specific overrides here -->
    </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

# global.json

The `global.json` file ensures all developers and CI systems use the same .NET SDK version, preventing version drift and build inconsistencies.

```json
{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100-preview.7",
    "rollForward": "latestMinor",
    "allowPrerelease": true
  }
}
```

**SDK Version Pinning**:
- **version**: Specific SDK version to use
- **rollForward**: How to handle version mismatches
- **allowPrerelease**: Whether to allow preview/beta versions

```json

    "version": "8.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestPatch"     // Use latest patch version

    // "rollForward": "latestMajor"   // Use latest major version

  }
}
```

- **Reproducible Builds**: Same SDK version across all environments
- **Feature Consistency**: All developers have access to the same language features
- **CI/CD Reliability**: Builds work identically in development and production
- **Version Drift Prevention**: Avoids "works on my machine" issues

```json
    "version": "9.0.100",           // Change to your preferred version

    "allowPrerelease": false        // Disable prerelease versions
  }
```

# nuget.config

The `nuget.config` file provides a complete package management strategy with environment-specific feeds and 
secure credential management using environment variables.

<Aside type="tip">
    Learn more about how we handle NuGet feeds and secrets in the [NuGet Feeds](../../nuget-feeds/nuget-feeds)
    and [NuGet Secrets](../../nuget-feeds/nuget-secrets) docs.    
</Aside>

## Configuration Structure

```xml
<configuration>
    <packageSources>
        <clear />
        <add key="Local" value="%NUGET_FEED_LOCAL_URL%" />
        <add key="Development" value="%NUGET_FEED_DEV_URL%" />
        <add key="Staging" value="%NUGET_FEED_STAGING_URL%" />
        <add key="Production" value="%NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_URL%" />
    </packageSources>

    <packageSourceCredentials>
        <Development>
            <add key="Username" value="%NUGET_FEED_DEV_USERNAME%" />
            <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%NUGET_FEED_DEV_PAT%" />
        </Development>
        <Staging>
            <add key="Username" value="%NUGET_FEED_STAGING_USERNAME%" />
            <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%NUGET_FEED_STAGING_PAT%" />
        </Staging>
        <Production>
            <add key="Username" value="%NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_USERNAME%" />
            <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%NUGET_FEED_PRODUCTION_PAT%" />
        </Production>
    </packageSourceCredentials>
</configuration>
```

## What It Configures

**Package Sources**:
- **Local**: Development packages stored locally
- **Development**: Internal development feed
- **Staging**: Pre-production package validation
- **Production**: Public or private production feed

**Authentication**:
- **Environment Variables**: Secure credential storage
- **Multiple Environments**: Different credentials per environment
- **Token-Based Auth**: Personal Access Tokens (PAT) for security


## Why This Matters

- **Environment Separation**: Clear boundaries between development stages
- **Security**: No hardcoded credentials in source control
- **Flexibility**: Easy to add/remove feeds without code changes
- **CI/CD Integration**: Different feeds for different pipeline stages

## Customizing nuget.config

To add a new feed or modify existing ones:

```xml
<configuration>
    <packageSources>
        <clear />
        <add key="Local" value="%NUGET_FEED_LOCAL_URL%" />
        <add key="Development" value="%NUGET_FEED_DEV_URL%" />
        <!-- Add your custom feed -->
        <add key="CustomFeed" value="https://your-custom-feed.com/v3/index.json" />
    </packageSources>

    <packageSourceCredentials>
        <!-- Add credentials for your custom feed -->
        <CustomFeed>
            <add key="Username" value="%CUSTOM_FEED_USERNAME%" />
            <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%CUSTOM_FEED_PAT%" />
        </CustomFeed>
    </packageSourceCredentials>
</configuration>
```

<Aside type="danger">
    **Warning**: Never commit actual credentials to source control. Always use environment variables.
</Aside>

# StyleCop Integration

The StyleCop configuration is located in the `stylecop.json` file in the solution root. This file enforces consistent code style and documentation standards across all C# projects.

## Configured Rules

The template configures only few of the following StyleCop rules in `stylecop.json`:

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "orderingRules": {
      "blankLinesBetweenUsingGroups": "omit"
    },
    "documentationRules": {
      "companyName": "Six",
      "copyrightText": "Copyright (c) {companyName}. All rights reserved.\nLicensed under the {licenseName} license. See {licenseFile} file in the project root for full license information.",
      "variables": {
        "licenseName": "MIT",
        "licenseFile": "License.txt"
      },
      "documentInternalElements": false,
      "documentationCulture": "en-GB"
    }
  }
}
```

### What Each Rule Does

- **blankLinesBetweenUsingGroups**: Controls spacing between using directive groups
- **companyName**: Sets the company name for copyright headers
- **copyrightText**: Defines the copyright text template with variables
- **variables**: Defines reusable variables for copyright text (license name and file)
- **documentInternalElements**: Whether to require documentation for internal elements
- **documentationCulture**: Culture for documentation text (en-GB)

## Disabling Specific Rules

To disable specific StyleCop rules for your project:

```xml
<!-- In Directory.Build.props -->
<PropertyGroup>
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);SA1600;SA1633</NoWarn>  <!-- Disable specific StyleCop warnings -->
</PropertyGroup>
```

The **Six Solution Template** establishes a clear, logical directory structure that organizes your .NET projects 
by purpose and type.

The template organizes projects into five main directories, each serving a specific purpose:

```
Six.SolutionTemplate/
├── libs/                    # Library projects (.csproj with type 'library')
├── apps/                    # Application projects (.csproj with type 'exe')
├── tests/                   # Test projects
├── benchmarks/              # Performance benchmark projects
└── docs/                    # In-repository documentation
```

## Directory.Build.props Inheritance

All directories use a hierarchical configuration system where settings cascade from root to specific directories:

### Configuration Hierarchy

1. **Root Directory.Build.props** - Base settings for all projects
2. **Directory-specific Directory.Build.props** - Specialized settings that extend the root
3. **Individual project files** - Final project-specific customizations


----

# Libs

The `libs/` directory contains all library projects that can be packaged as NuGet packages.

## Directory Structure

```
libs/
├── Directory.Build.props       # Library-specific configuration
├── Directory.Build.targets     # Library-specific build targets
└── [ProjectName]/
    ├── src/                    # Source code
    ├── project_icon.png        # Package icon (128x128 recommended)
    ├── README.md               # Package documentation
    └── GlobalUsings.cs         # Global using statements
```

The `libs/Directory.Build.props` file configures library-specific settings:

```xml

    <!-- Library-specific properties -->
    <IsPackable>true</IsPackable>
    <GeneratePackageOnBuild>false</GeneratePackageOnBuild>
    <IncludeSymbols>true</IncludeSymbols>
    <SymbolPackageFormat>snupkg</SymbolPackageFormat>

    <!-- Package metadata defaults -->
    <PackageLicenseExpression>MIT</PackageLicenseExpression>
    <PackageRequireLicenseAcceptance>false</PackageRequireLicenseAcceptance>
    <Authors>Six Technology</Authors>
    <Company>Six Technology</Company>

    <!-- Source Link for debugging -->
    <PublishRepositoryUrl>true</PublishRepositoryUrl>
    <EmbedUntrackedSources>true</EmbedUntrackedSources>
</Project>
```

<Aside type="note">
    The `nuget-pack.cs` script automatically scans the `libs/` directory to discover and package all library projects.
</Aside>


----

# Apps

The `apps/` directory contains all application projects including console apps, web APIs, web applications, desktop applications, etc.

## Directory Structure

```
apps/
├── Directory.Build.props       # Application-specific configuration
└── [ProjectName]/
    ├── src/                    # Source code
    ├── project_icon.png        # Application icon
    ├── README.md               # Application documentation
    ├── GlobalUsings.cs         # Global using statements
```

# Overview

The **Six.SolutionTemplate** includes a comprehensive set of **Cursor rules** organized in the `.cursor/rules/` directory.
These rules provide detailed guidance for AI-assisted development, ensuring consistent code quality, proper architectural
patterns, and streamlined development workflows across different technologies and development scenarios.

Cursor rules are configuration files (`.mdc` format) that help AI coding assistants understand your project's specific requirements,
coding standards, and best practices. They act as a bridge between your development team's knowledge and AI tools,
ensuring consistent and high-quality code generation.

## Hierarchical Organization

The rules are organized hierarchically by technology and purpose, making it easy to find and apply the right guidance for your development context:

```
.cursor/rules/
├── dotnet/                   # .NET development rules
│   ├── aspnet/               # ASP.NET Core API development
│   ├── avalonia/             # Avalonia desktop applications
│   ├── blazor/               # Blazor web applications
│   ├── ci-cd/                # CI/CD workflows and automation
│   ├── csharp/               # C# language and coding standards
│   └── general/              # General .NET patterns and practices
├── web/                      # Web development rules
│   ├── astro/                # Astro.js framework development
│   └── typescript/           # TypeScript development standards
├── documentation/            # Documentation best practices
│   ├── agents-md.mdc         # AI agent documentation standards
│   ├── readme-md.md          # README file best practices
│   └── tech-writer.md        # Steering for technical writing
└── specs-generation/         # Specification-driven development
    └── coding-by-spec.mdc    # Spec-driven development patterns
```


## How Rules Work

### Automatic Application
Rules are automatically applied by Cursor based on:
- **File patterns**: Rules target specific file types using glob patterns (e.g., `**/*.cs`, `**/*.ts`, `**/*.mdx`)
- **Directory context**: Rules apply when working in relevant project directories
- **Project structure**: Rules activate based on detected frameworks and project configuration
- **Always-apply settings**: Some rules can be configured to always apply regardless of context

### Manual Reference
You can explicitly reference rules in your prompts using the hierarchical path structure:
```
@.cursor/rules/dotnet/csharp/csharp-coding-style.mdc Create a user service
@.cursor/rules/web/typescript/typescript-coding-style.mdc Implement validation
```

### Rule Combinations
Multiple rules can work together:
```
@.cursor/rules/dotnet/aspnet/aspnet-api.mdc @.cursor/rules/dotnet/general/dotnet-testing.mdc Create an API with tests
```

### Rule File Format
All rules use the `.mdc` (Markdown with Cursor) format, which includes:
- **Frontmatter metadata**: Description, file patterns, and application settings
- **Structured content**: Role definitions, requirements, and detailed guidance
- **Practical examples**: Code samples showing both recommended and discouraged patterns
- **Integration guidance**: How rules work together and complement each other

Overview of the Kiro steering system and how AI assistants use them for consistent, high-quality code generation

# Overview

The **Six.SolutionTemplate** includes a comprehensive set of **Kiro steering files** organized in the `.kiro/steering/` directory.
These steering files provide detailed guidance for AI-assisted development, ensuring consistent code quality, proper architectural
patterns, and streamlined development workflows across different technologies and development scenarios.

Kiro steering files are configuration files (`.md` format) that help AI coding assistants understand your project's specific requirements,
coding standards, and best practices. They act as a bridge between your development team's knowledge and AI tools,
ensuring consistent and high-quality code generation.

## Hierarchical Organization

The steering files are organized hierarchically by technology and purpose, making it easy to find and apply the 
right guidance for your development context:

```
.kiro/steering/
├── dotnet/                   # .NET development steering files
│   ├── aspnet/               # ASP.NET Core API development
│   ├── avalonia/             # Avalonia desktop applications
│   ├── blazor/               # Blazor web applications
│   ├── ci-cd/                # CI/CD workflows and automation
│   ├── csharp/               # C# language and coding standards
│   └── general/              # General .NET patterns and practices
├── web/                      # Web development steering files
│   ├── astro/                # Astro.js framework development
│   └── typescript/           # TypeScript development standards
└── documentation/            # Documentation best practices
    ├── agents-md.md          # AI agent documentation standards
    ├── readme-md.md          # README file best practices
    └── tech-writer.md        # Steering for technical writing
```


## How Steering Files Work

### Automatic Application
Steering files are automatically applied by Kiro based on:
- **File patterns**: Steering files target specific file types using glob patterns (e.g., `**/*.cs`, `**/*.ts`, `**/*.mdx`)
- **Directory context**: Steering files apply when working in relevant project directories
- **Project structure**: Steering files activate based on detected frameworks and project configuration
- **Always-apply settings**: Some steering files can be configured to always apply regardless of context

### Manual Reference
You can explicitly reference steering files in your prompts using the hierarchical path structure:
```
#[[file:.kiro/steering/dotnet/csharp/csharp-coding-style.md]] Create a user service
#[[file:.kiro/steering/web/typescript/typescript-coding-style.md]] Implement validation
```

### Steering File Combinations
Multiple steering files can work together:
```
#[[file:.kiro/steering/dotnet/aspnet/aspnet-api.md]] #[[file:.kiro/steering/dotnet/general/dotnet-testing.md]] Create an API with tests
```

### Steering File Format
All steering files use the `.md` (Markdown) format, which includes:
- **Frontmatter metadata**: Description, file patterns, and application settings
- **Structured content**: Role definitions, requirements, and detailed guidance
- **Practical examples**: Code samples showing both recommended and discouraged patterns
- **Integration guidance**: How steering files work together and complement each other

## Kiro Hooks System

In addition to steering files, Kiro includes a powerful **hooks system** that enables automated workflow triggers:

- **Event-Driven Automation**: Hooks respond to file changes, user actions, and other development events
- **AI Agent Integration**: Hooks can automatically trigger AI agent actions with specific prompts
- **Workflow Enhancement**: Automate documentation updates, code analysis, and development workflows
- **Context-Aware Actions**: Hooks provide relevant context to AI agents for better task execution

Learn more about the [Kiro Hooks System](https://kiro.dev/docs/hooks/).
